The new name of the income tax law for 2025 is the Income-tax Act, 2025.  
(Source: Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement)

The Income-tax Act, 2025 shall come into force on the 1st April, 2026.  
(Source: Section 1(3) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

No, if you are not ordinarily resident in India and earn money from a business outside India, you do not have to include it in your income under Section 9 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, provided that the income accrues or arises outside India and is not deemed to accrue or arise in India.

Source: Section 9(14) – "Income from foreign sources" means income which accrues or arises outside India (except income derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India) and which is not deemed to accrue or arise in India.

Note: The income will only be deemed to accrue or arise in India if there is a business connection in India (as defined in Section 9), such as a significant economic presence or business carried out in India. If there is no such connection, income from a business outside India is not included in income.

No, income that is received in India through a balance sheet prepared in India does not count as income received in India for tax purposes.

Source: Section 5(3) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states: "Income accruing or arising outside India shall not be deemed to be received in India under this section by reason only of the fact that it is taken into account in a balance sheet prepared in India."

Yes, if you are a citizen of India and visit India for a short period, you will still be considered a resident in India for tax purposes.  

Source: Section 6(4) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that the provisions of sub-section (2)(b) shall not apply to an individual who is a citizen of India or a person of Indian origin and who is outside India but comes on a visit to India in any tax year. This means that such an individual is deemed to be resident in India for that tax year, regardless of the duration of their visit.  

Additionally, Section 6(13) and Section 6(7) further confirm that citizens of India are generally resident in India, especially when their income exceeds fifteen lakh rupees (excluding foreign sources), or when they are deemed to be resident under specific conditions.  

Thus, being a citizen of India and visiting India for a short period does not negate residency for tax purposes.

Yes, if your total income from sources in India exceeds 15 lakh rupees during a tax year (excluding income from foreign sources), you will be considered a resident in India, even if you are not physically present in India for a long time.  

This is based on Section 6(7) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that an individual shall be deemed to be resident in India if:  
(a) they are a citizen of India;  
(b) they are not liable to tax in any other country or territory due to their domicile, residence, or similar criteria; and  
(c) their total income (other than income from foreign sources) exceeds fifteen lakh rupees during the tax year.  

Additionally, Section 6(5) provides that if a citizen of India or a person of Indian origin has total income exceeding fifteen lakh rupees (excluding foreign sources), the provisions of sub-section (2)(b) shall apply as if the words “sixty days” had been substituted with “one hundred and twenty days,” further reinforcing the link between income level and residency status.  

Source: Section 6(7) and Section 6(5), Income-Tax Act 2025.

Dividend income is considered to be received for tax purposes in the tax year in which it is declared, distributed, or paid, as the case may be. This is specified in Section 7(2)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. Additionally, an interim dividend is deemed to be the income of the tax year in which the amount is unconditionally made available to the entitled member. 

Source: Section 7(2)(a) and (b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, an interim dividend is taxed in the year it is made available to shareholders.  

Source: Section 7(2)(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, their income will not be taxed together.  
Source: Section 10(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Under Section 10 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, if one spouse earns salary and the other does not, the salary income shall be included in the total income of the spouse who has actually earned it.  

**Source:** Section 10(a)(d) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, certain types of income will be ignored when calculating your total taxable income. Under Section 11 of the Income-Tax Act 2025, incomes enumerated in Schedules II, III, IV, V, and VI are not included in total income, subject to fulfilment of specified conditions. If these conditions are not met, such income shall be charged to tax. Additionally, incomes of persons enumerated in Schedule VII are not chargeable to tax if conditions are fulfilled; otherwise, they are taxable. 

Source: Section 11: Incomes not included in total income.

Yes, if a political party or electoral trust doesn't meet the conditions mentioned in Schedule VIII, such income shall be charged to tax under the Income-Tax Act for that tax year.  
(Source: Section 12(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, salary includes payments made for unused leave.  

Source: Section 16( h) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that "any payment received by an employee in respect of any period of leave not availed of by him" is included in "salary".

Yes, the annual increase in a provident fund balance is considered part of salary for tax purposes.  

Source: Section 16(1)(h) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that "salary" includes "the annual accretion to the balance at the credit of an employee participating in a recognised provident fund, to the extent to which it is chargeable to tax as per paragraph 6 of Part A of Schedule XI."  

This indicates that the annual accretion (increase) is included in salary for tax purposes, subject to the conditions specified in Schedule XI.

The amount of arrears of rent received in the current year, or the unrealised rent realised subsequently from a tenant, shall be deemed to be the income from house property in respect of the tax year in which such rent is received or realised. This amount shall be included in the total income of the assessee under the head “Income from house property”, whether the assessee is the owner of the property or not in that tax year. A sum equal to 30% of such arrears or unrealised rent shall be allowed as deduction.

(Source: Section 23(1) and (3) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, you can claim a deduction of 30% when you receive overdue rent or rent that was unrealised but collected later.  

Source: Section 23(3) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that "A sum equal to 30% of the arrears of rent or the unrealised rent referred to in sub-section (1) shall be allowed as deduction."

Yes, there are exceptions when calculating profits from a business or profession related to rent, rates, taxes, repairs, and insurance.

- Under **Section 28(1)(c)**, rent paid when the premises are occupied by the assessee as a tenant is deductible, but only if it is for premises used in the business or profession.  
- Under **Section 28(2)**, if the premises, machinery, plant, or furniture is partly or not wholly used for business, the deduction is restricted to the fair proportionate part as determined by the Assessing Officer.  
- Under **Section 55**, profits from an insurance business are computed under **Schedule XIV**, irrespective of other provisions (including Sections 26 to 54), which means insurance-related profits are not computed under the general rules of Sections 28 to 60 (except Section 58).  

Thus, the exceptions are:  
1. **Part-use limitation** under Section 28(2) for premises, machinery, plant, or furniture.  
2. **Special computation under Schedule XIV** for insurance business under Section 55.  

(Source: Section 28(2), Section 55)

Yes, an employer can deduct contributions made to a pension scheme for employees if such contributions are up to 14% of the employee's salary, including dearness allowance, provided that the terms of employment so provide.  

Source: Section 29(1)(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, there is no specific limit mentioned on how much an employer can contribute to a gratuity fund under the provided context. 

However, Section 29(1)(c) allows deduction for contributions towards an approved gratuity fund created by the employer for the exclusive benefit of employees under an irrevocable trust, subject to conditions specified by the Board. Section 536( h) deals with the tax exemption on payments from a superannuation fund from which approval has been withdrawn, but does not specify contribution limits. 

The context does not explicitly state a cap or limit on employer contributions to a gratuity fund. Therefore, based on the provided information, **there is no limit specified** on employer contributions to a gratuity fund. 

(Source: Section 29(1)(c) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, you can claim depreciation for buildings or machinery that are only used part of the time for your business, but the deduction shall be restricted to the fair proportionate part thereof as determined by the Assessing Officer, having regard to the usage of such building, machinery, plant, or furniture for the purposes of the business or profession.

Source: Section 33(3)(b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, expenses for paying a bribe or violating a law are not allowed as business expenses.  

Source: Section 34(2)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that an expenditure incurred for any purpose which is an offence or is prohibited by law shall not be allowed as a deduction. Additionally, Section 353(f) specifies that such expenditure is not allowable if it is not in the form of a contribution or donation and is not on account of a payment made in contravention of section 36.  

Thus, payments that violate law or constitute an offence are not deductible.

No, you cannot claim a deduction for employer contributions to a provident fund in the year you actually pay it if the liability was incurred in a previous year.

Source: Section 29(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that deductions are allowed for contributions towards a recognised provident fund, subject to prescribed limits and conditions. However, this section does not specify that contributions incurred in a previous year can be claimed in the year of payment. The provision allows deductions only for contributions made during the tax year, and the conditions (such as annual contributions fixed on a definite basis) imply that contributions must be made in the relevant assessment year to be deductible. Since the context does not explicitly permit carry-forward or claim of deductions for contributions incurred in a prior year, and no such provision is stated, the deduction is only allowable for contributions made in the tax year.

Therefore, based on the provided context, contributions incurred in a previous year cannot be claimed as a deduction in the year of payment.

Yes, you can claim a deduction for expenses like market surveys or feasibility reports when starting a new business in India, provided they are wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession.

Source: Section 34(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which allows deduction for expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business or profession.

Yes, you can claim a tax deduction for expenses on an agricultural extension project, provided the project is notified by the Board as per the guidelines issued by it. The expenditure (excluding cost of land or building) incurred on such a project shall be allowed as a deduction in the tax year in which it is incurred.  

Source: Section 47(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, if you claim a deduction for a skill development project under Section 47, you cannot claim the same expenditure as a deduction under any other provision of the Income-Tax Act for the same tax year.  

Source: Section 47(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, you can get a tax deduction if you deposit money into a special account for growing tea, coffee, or rubber in India.  

Under **Section 48(1)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, an assessee carrying on business of growing and manufacturing tea, coffee, or rubber in India is allowed a deduction based on deposits into a special account or deposit account, as computed per the provisions of **Schedule IX**.  

Additionally, **Schedule X** specifies that the deduction is either (a) the amount deposited in the specified account or (b) 20% of the profits of the business before any loss set-off, whichever is less.  

**Source:** Section 48(1) and Schedule X.

Yes, if you have a deal with the government to explore or produce oil or gas in India, you can get a tax deduction for money put into a site restoration account. This is provided under Section 49(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which allows a deduction on the basis of deposits into a special account or site restoration account, computed as per the provisions of Schedule X. 

Source: Section 49(1) – Site Restoration Fund.

Yes, if you sell an asset acquired under a government special scheme, the sale will be taxed in the year of the sale, but only if the asset is sold or transferred to any person in the tax year before the expiry of eight years from the end of the tax year in which it was acquired.

According to Section 536(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, the part of the cost of the asset relatable to the deduction allowed under paragraph 1 shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of business of the tax year in which such asset is sold or transferred, and shall accordingly be charged to income-tax for that tax year.

However, this does not apply if the asset is sold or transferred by the assessee to the specified person (such as the Government, a local authority, or a corporation established by or under a Central, State or Provincial Act), or if a firm transfers it to a company under specific conditions related to succession of business or profession.

Source: Section 536(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, if the amount received from the sale of land is less than the stamp duty value, the stamp duty value can be used to calculate the profit, subject to certain conditions.

Under **Section 78(1)(a)** of the Income-Tax Act 2025, if the consideration received or accruing from the transfer of land or building is less than the stamp duty value, the stamp duty value shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration for the purposes of section 72 (which relates to computation of profit and gains). However, this applies only if:

- The date of agreement fixing the consideration and the date of registration are not the same; and  
- Part or full consideration is received on or before the date of agreement in "specified banking or online mode" as defined in section 66(32).

Additionally, if the stamp duty value does not exceed 110% of the consideration received or accruing, the consideration itself shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration (Section 78(1)(b)).

Thus, the stamp duty value may be used to compute profit when the consideration is less than the stamp duty value, provided the conditions in Section 78(1) are met.  

**Source: Section 78(1)(a) and (b)**

Yes, you can use the amount you actually received when selling a building as the full value of consideration if the stamp duty value is under 110% of what you received, provided the consideration received or accrued is less than the stamp duty value.

Source: Section 53(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025. This section states that if the stamp duty value does not exceed 110% of the consideration received or accrued, such consideration shall be deemed to be the full value of consideration.

Yes, you can get a deduction for expenses spent on exploration before starting commercial production.  

This is provided under **Section 54: Business of prospecting for mineral oils**, sub-section (3)(a), which states that for the period before the beginning of commercial production, expenditure towards infructuous or abortive exploration incurred in respect of any surrendered area shall be allowed as a deduction.  

**Source: Section 54(3)(a)**

If you transfer your oil exploration business, the profit or deduction is calculated as follows:

- Let A = proceeds of the transfer (so far as they consist of capital sums);  
- B = total amount of expenditure incurred in connection with the business or to obtain interest therein;  
- C = amount of expenditure incurred remaining unallowed.

Then:

(a) If A is less than C, then (C – A) shall be allowed as deduction in the tax year of transfer.  
(b) If A is greater than C:  
(i) But less than B, then (A – C) shall be the profit chargeable under the head “Profits and gains of business or profession” for the tax year of transfer;  
(ii) In any other case, only (B – C) shall be the profit chargeable under the said head for the tax year of transfer.  
(iii) No deduction shall be allowed for expenditure incurred remaining unallowed in the tax year of transfer or any subsequent tax year.

(Source: Section 54, Income-Tax Act 2025)

Interest income from bad or doubtful debts of a scheduled bank is considered taxable in the tax year in which such interest is **credited to the profit and loss account or actually received, whichever is earlier**.  

(Source: Section 56(1)(a) and (b) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, a co-operative bank falls under the special tax rule for interest on bad debts.  

Source: Section 56(2)(iii) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which defines "specified financial institution" to include a co-operative bank, other than a primary agricultural credit society or a primary co-operative agricultural and rural development bank. Since bad or doubtful debts interest is governed under Section 56, and co-operative banks (excluding specified exceptions) are included in the definition of "specified financial institution," they are subject to the special tax rule for interest income on bad or doubtful debts.  

Thus, co-operative banks (excluding the excluded types) are covered under Section 56.
When a service contract lasts less than 90 days, profit is calculated on the basis of the project completion method, as per Section 57(2)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, retention money counts towards contract revenue when using the percentage of completion method.  
Source: Section 57(3)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, a non-resident cannot deduct head office expenses incurred outside India when calculating their business income in India.

Source: Section 60(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that deduction of head office expenditure incurred by a non-resident assessee as attributable to his business or profession in India is allowed in computing income chargeable under the head “Profits and gains of business or profession”. However, the section specifically defines “head office expenditure” as executive and general administration expenditure incurred in respect of premises outside India, salary, wages, travelling, and other matters connected with executive and general administration. Thus, such expenses incurred outside India are eligible for deduction only if they are attributable to business or profession in India.

But note: The section does not allow deduction of head office expenses incurred outside India for the purpose of computing income from business in India — rather, it allows deduction only if the expenses are attributable to business in India. Since the expenses are incurred outside India, and the business connection is in India, the deduction is allowed only under specific conditions and is subject to the upper monetary limit of 5% of adjusted total income.

Therefore, based on the context, head office expenses incurred outside India are eligible for deduction only if they are attributable to business in India, and such deduction is subject to the 5% cap under Section 60(2). Hence, the deduction is possible under certain conditions, but not automatically.

Final answer: Yes, a non-resident can deduct head office expenses incurred outside India when calculating their business income in India, subject to the conditions in Section 60(1) and (2), including the 5% upper monetary limit on such deductions.

Source: Section 60: Deduction of head office expenditure in case of non-residents (Income-Tax Act 2025).

The maximum limit for deducting head office expenses for a non-resident if their total income is a loss is 5% of the average adjusted total income of the assessee.  

Source: Section 60(2)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, you need to keep proper books of account if you run a business or profession, provided that your income from business or profession exceeds ₹120,000 or your total sales, turnover, or gross receipts exceed ten lakh rupees in any one of the three years immediately preceding the tax year. Additionally, if the business or profession is newly set up and is likely to exceed these thresholds, or if the assessee has claimed income lower than the deemed profits, then books of account must be maintained. For individuals or Hindu Undivided Families, the thresholds are higher: income exceeding ₹250,000 or gross receipts exceeding twenty-five lakh rupees.  

Source: Section 62(1)(b) and (2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, if you are a doctor or lawyer, you are required to maintain books of account even if your income is below certain limits.  

**Source:** Section 62(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that "any person carrying on specified profession" (including legal, medical, engineering, architectural, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, information technology or company secretary) shall keep and maintain such books of account and other documents to enable the Assessing Officer to compute his total income.  

This obligation applies regardless of income level, as the category of "specified profession" is explicitly defined and includes doctors and lawyers.  

Thus, as a doctor or lawyer, you must maintain books of account under Section 62(1)(a), irrespective of income.

Yes, you still need to get your books audited if your business turnover exceeds one crore rupees, even if most of your payments and receipts are made by cheque or bank draft.

Source: Section 63(5) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that "the payment or receipt, as the case may be, by a cheque drawn on a bank or by a bank draft, which is not account payee, shall be deemed to be the payment or receipt, as the case may be, in cash." This means that even if transactions are made via cheque or bank draft, if they are not account payee, they are treated as cash for the purpose of determining the threshold for tax audit.

Additionally, Section 63(1)(a) requires that a person carrying on a business with total sales, turnover, or gross receipts exceeding one crore rupees in a tax year must get their accounts audited.

Therefore, since your turnover exceeds one crore, and the nature of payments (cheques/bank drafts not being account payee) is treated as cash, the condition for tax audit applies.

Final Answer: Yes, you need to get your books audited because your turnover exceeds one crore rupees, and payments/receipts not being account payee are deemed to be in cash, triggering the audit requirement under Section 63(1)(a) and Section 63(5).

Yes, if your profession income exceeds fifty lakh rupees in any tax year, you are required to get your accounts audited, even if you do not have any cash transactions.  

**Source:** Section 63(1)(c) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that a person carrying on a profession shall get his accounts audited if his gross receipts in profession exceed fifty lakh rupees in any tax year. This requirement is independent of cash transactions.

Yes, a transfer of shares during a company merger is not considered a taxable event if the new company is in India, as per Section 70(1)(e) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that in a scheme of amalgamation, a transfer of a capital asset by the amalgamating company to the amalgamated company is not regarded as a transfer if the amalgamated company is an Indian company. 

Source: Section 70: Transactions not regarded as transfer (Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, a foreign company can transfer shares in India to another foreign company without capital gains tax if at least 25% of the original shareholders continue to remain shareholders of the resulting foreign company and the transfer does not attract tax on capital gains in the country where the foreign company is incorporated.  

Source: Section 70( h) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

The cost of acquisition for capital gains calculation will be the original cost of the share, adjusted for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index (CII).  

Source: Section 90(iv)(B) and (C) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that for equity shares that were not listed on a recognised stock exchange as on 31st January, 2018 but became listed subsequently or were acquired in a transaction not regarded as a transfer, the cost of acquisition is adjusted in proportion to the Cost Inflation Index for the tax year 2017-18 compared to the CII for the first year of holding or the year beginning 1st April, 2001, whichever is later.  

Thus, even if the fair market value is higher than the original cost, the cost of acquisition for capital gains is adjusted based on the CII, not the fair market value.

No, personal expenses cannot be deducted when calculating income from other sources.  

Source: Section 94(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that "any personal expenses of the assessee" shall not be deductible in computing the income chargeable under the head "Income from other sources".

No, you cannot claim deductions for expenses related to maintaining the horses if you earn money from horse races, because under Section 94(4), no deduction for any expenditure or allowance related to income from winnings from horse races, card games, or gambling is allowed.  

However, Section 115(4)(d) defines "specified activity" as the activity of owning and maintaining race horses, and allows a loss incurred in such activity to be set off against income from the same activity. This means that if your income from horse races is less than your expenditure (excluding capital expenditure), you may claim a loss that can be set off against future income from the same activity.  

But note: Section 94(4) explicitly prohibits deductions for expenses related to winnings from horse races, so such expenses cannot be deducted in computing income from winnings.  

Source: Section 94(4) and Section 115(4)(d) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

If you can't explain where your expenses came from, the amount of such expenditure shall be deemed to be your income for that tax year.  
(Source: Section 105(1)(a) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, you cannot deduct expenses that you did not explain or could not justify as coming from a legitimate source.  

Source: Section 105(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that if an assessee offers no explanation about the source of expenditure or the explanation is not satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure shall be deemed to be income and shall not be allowed as a deduction.  

Additionally, Section 105(2) clarifies that such deemed income shall not be allowed as a deduction under the Act.

Yes, if you borrow money through a hundi or a cheque that is not payable to a specific account holder (i.e., not an account payee cheque), the amount borrowed (including interest) is considered income for the tax year in which it was borrowed.

Source: Section 106(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, you will not have to pay tax again on the amount repaid through a hundi when you pay it back.

Source: Section 106(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025 states that where the amount borrowed under sub-section (1) has been deemed to be the income of any person, such person shall not be liable to be assessed again in respect of such amount on repayment of such amount.

No. A loss from a short-term capital asset cannot be used to offset gains from a long-term capital asset.

Source: Section 111(1)(a)(i) and (ii) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.  
According to Section 111(1)(a)(i), a loss from a short-term capital asset can only be set off against income from other short-term capital assets. Similarly, a loss from a long-term capital asset can only be set off against income from other long-term capital assets. Therefore, cross-setoff between short-term and long-term capital assets is not permitted.

Under Section 111(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, no loss shall be carried forward under this section for more than eight tax years immediately succeeding the tax year for which the loss was first computed.  

Source: Section 111(2)

No. According to Section 114(1), a loss computed in respect of a specified business can only be set off against profits and gains of another specified business. Therefore, you can use a loss from one specified business to offset profits from a different specified business.  
(Source: Section 114(1))

Yes, if you don’t fully use your loss from a specified business in a year, you can carry it forward to the next year to be set off against future profits.  

Source: Section 114(2)(i) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

No, if a public sector company sells its shares and loses control (i.e., undergoes strategic disinvestment), its accumulated losses cannot be passed on to another company after merging, unless specific conditions are met.

According to Section 119( f) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, losses of an "erstwhile public sector company" cannot be set off or carried forward to another company if, after the strategic disinvestment, the ultimate holding company continues to hold at least 51% of the voting power of the company. 

Additionally, Section 116(1)(d) provides that in cases of amalgamation involving an erstwhile public sector company, the accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation of the amalgamating company are deemed to be those of the amalgamated company, but only if the share purchase agreement restricted immediate amalgamation and the amalgamation occurs within five years of the restriction ending. However, such deemed losses are capped at the level of the public sector company’s accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation on the date it ceases to be a public sector company.

Crucially, Section 119(5) states that if the conditions in sub-section (4)(f) are not complied with (i.e., if the ultimate holding company does not hold at least 51% of voting power), then the provisions of sub-section (3) apply, which generally restrict the set-off or carry-forward of losses.

Therefore, **losses cannot be passed on** unless the ultimate holding company retains at least 51% of voting power post-disinvestment. If control is lost and this condition is not met, losses are not transferable.

Source: Section 119( f) and Section 119(5) of the Income-Tax Act 2025.

Yes, in a demerger, if the old company's losses are directly linked to the business transferred, they can be carried forward and set off in the hands of the resulting company.  

Source: Section 116: or demerger, etc — Sub-section (6)(a) states that "if directly relatable to the undertakings transferred to the resulting company, be allowed to be carried forward and set off in the hands of the resulting company."

Yes, you can get a tax deduction for the amount you paid into the Agnipath Scheme's fund after November 1, 2022.  

Source: Section 125(1) of the Income-Tax Act 2025, which states that an individual who has enrolled in the Agnipath Scheme and subscribes to the Agniveer Corpus Fund on or after November 1, 2022, shall be allowed a deduction in the computation of his total income of the whole amount paid or deposited in the Fund during the tax year.

Yes, if the Central Government makes a contribution to the account of an assessee in the Agniveer Corpus Fund, the assessee shall be allowed a deduction in the computation of his total income of the whole of the amount so contributed.  
(Source: Section 125(2) of the Income-Tax Act 2025)

Yes, you can claim a tax deduction for health insurance paid for your parents if they are senior citizens.
